theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon
notes: Watkins's Basic Formula *(é)gʷʰent ógʷʰim. Past of the root present (Ved. imperfect áhan, Av. janat̰, Hitt. preterite kuenta); Greek has the reduplicated aorist (κατ)έπεφνε of the same root and ὄφις in Pindar (not in the local Homer corpus; Il. 6.183 is Bellerophon slaying the Chimaera). The engine prints the augmentless form, which Watkins allows. Verb-initial order follows Vedic and Avestan; Hittite is verb-final. Hittite illuyanka- is not a cognate of *h₁ógʷʰis.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: He it is who slew the serpent.

notes: Watkins's relative-clause definition of the hero ('who slew the serpent', Y. 9.8, Yt. 19.40; RV 2.12 refrain sá janāsa índraḥ). Relative *yo- (Ved. yá-, Av. ya-, Gk. ὅς) with a *gʷʰen- past in all three; *h₁ógʷʰis is Indo-Iranian only here. Vedic has the perfect jaghā́na, Avestan janat̰: the past of the present stem is chosen to match the Basic Formula. The copular main clause is interpolated (Vedic sá ... índraḥ has a noun predicate instead).

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon
notes: Second lexical variant of the formula, *terh₂- 'overcome' (Watkins ch. 34), here with the monster as subject (the serpent's first, temporary victory over the Storm God). Hittite tarḫu- is a u-stem present, matching the lexeme térh₂uti; the Vedic counterpart is the negated aorist (Vṛtra 'did not withstand' Indra's weapons), so the two branches agree on root and roles but not on polarity. The serpent is interpolated (Hitt. illuyanka- is not cognate; the Vedic subject is Vṛtra, called áhi- in 1.32.5). Clause-initial nu is Hittite nu=za.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon
notes: The *terh₂- formula in the other direction: the Storm God 'began to overcome' the serpent (Hittite periphrasis with dai-, rendered as a simple past); Vedic tū́rvasi and Avestan tauruuaiia- show the same u-extended root as Hittite tarḫu-. The object 'serpent' is interpolated (Hitt. illuyanka-, Ved. vṛtrá- are not cognates of *h₁ógʷʰis).

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: Let them overcome him, let them thrust at him, and let them put him at their own feet.

notes: Watkins ch. 33: the Luvian imprecation 'may the gods crush him like reeds, smash him, put him under their feet' (*terh₂-, *wedʰ(h₁)-, *ped-, *dʰeh₁-) against RV 1.32.6-8 (nā́tārīd ... vadhā́nām; like a split reed; at the feet lay the serpent). Reduplicated present for Luvian tatarḫ- (cf. Ved. titar-); imperative 3pl matches Luvian -ndu. The *wedʰh₁- lexeme is glossed 'push, thrust' (LIV), so the English says 'thrust'; Vedic vadh- means 'smite'. The reed simile (*nedo-) and 'under' (Luv. annan) are left out: no usable lexemes. dʰeh₁- 'put' is Luvian only; 'their own' (swos) is interpolated.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon
notes: Watkins ch. 53 (SLAY ... LIE): the slain adversary lies. *ḱey- 'lie' (Ved. śáye, Av. sōire, Gk. κεῖμαι) and the verbal adjective *gʷʰn̥tó- (Av. jata-, Gk. -φατος in πρόσφατος 'newly slain'; Ved. hatá- in RV 10.108.4). The Greek passage is Hekabe over Hector, not a monster; *h₁ógʷʰis is Vedic only here.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: He slew the serpent lying there.

notes: RV 2.12.11 'who slew the serpent, the Dānu, lying (there)': accusative *h₁ógʷʰim with the middle participle *ḱéymh₁nom, exactly Ved. áhiṃ ... śáyānam = Gk. ὄφιν κείμενον (Il. 12.208, the snake dropped by the eagle, lying amid the Trojans). The Greek snake is a portent, not a slain dragon; Greek *gʷʰen- is cited from the Chimaera episode (Il. 6.183). Vedic has the perfect jaghā́na; the past of the root present is chosen as in the Basic Formula.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: Now the serpent lies; it sleeps.

notes: Watkins ch. 54 (LIE ... SLEEP): the slain dragon 'lies, sleeps' (Beowulf of the dragon; Indra 'put to sleep' Vṛtra lying in the streams). *swep- 'sleep' is in both (OE swefan, Ved. svap-); 'lie' is *legʰ- in Old English but *ḱey- in Vedic: *ḱey- is chosen with the Vedic, so it is not secure. The serpent is interpolated (OE wyrm < *wr̥mis, Ved. vṛtrá-). nu: OE nū (also Ved. nú), a closed particle.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: He bound the serpent with a rope.

notes: Ḫupašiya binds the serpent with a rope (Hitt. išḫiman- = OE sīma, the lexeme sh₂imṓ; Gk. ἱμάς, ἱμάσσω are from the same root *sh₂ey-, the Greek thong with which Zeus lashes the earth around Typhoeus). The verb: Ved. si- (nasal present sinā́ti, Varuṇa's binding, RV 7.84.2) and OE sǣlan 'bind (with rope)' are from the same root; Hittite uses kaleliya-, Greek δέω. Old English is Genesis B (the bound adversary), not in the local corpus. The serpent is interpolated (Hitt. illuyanka- is not cognate). Root-mate sh₂éymn̥ 'rope' (Greek, Celtic reflexes) not used.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: You became the striker of the serpent.

notes: Watkins ch. 43: Germanic 'become the bane' (ON at bana verða, OE tō banan weorðan) as the periphrastic continuant of *gʷʰen-, with the agent noun *gʷʰonós = Ved. ghaná- 'striker'; Vedic has the same construction, 'you became the striker of the vṛtras' (RV 1.4.8, cf. 8.96.18). Grípisspá 11: Sigurðr will slay the serpent Fáfnir. 'Become' is *bʰuH- with the Vedic (Gmc. verða is *wert-, Gk. γένοντο *ǵenh₁-), so not secure. Greek φόνος is the action noun (lexeme gʷʰónos-2), not this agent noun. 'Serpent' is interpolated (Ved. vṛtrá-, ON ormr < *wr̥mis).

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: He who slays, he is slain.

notes: The slayer slain (Watkins ch. 31): OIr gonas géntar 'who slays will be slain', Welsh ef wanei wanwyd 'he who would slay was slain', both *gʷʰen- active then passive; RV 8.84.9 'whom none slay, who slays' has the same root in both clauses with the relative yá-. The passive is rendered by the middle (OIr has a future passive, Welsh a preterite impersonal): an interpolated voice choice. Celtic is two languages but one branch.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: With the striker I slay the serpent.

notes: The Basic Formula as performative charm, 1st person present (Watkins ch. 56): Atharvavedic 'with the striker I slay' (in a charm against snakes, the object a real snake: Watkins) and the Old Irish worm charm 'I slay the creature' (gono míl). Shared: *gʷʰen- 1sg present (Ved. hanmi, OIr gono). The instrument ghaná- (*gʷʰonós) and the snake object are Vedic only (AV not in the local corpus) (OIr míl 'animal' has no usable lexeme).

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: He slew the serpent, and the gods were with him.

notes: HERO SLAY SERPENT with COMPANION (Watkins ch. 36): the Storm God slew the serpent 'and the gods were with him' (Hittite), Indra slew the serpent 'accompanied by Viṣṇu' (Vedic), Bellerophon slew the Chimaera trusting the gods' portents (Greek). Secure is *gʷʰen- only. Hittite DINGIRMEŠ (read šiuneš < *dyew-) is a logogram, so *deywós is interpolated; Hitt. ešer 'they were' (*h₁és-) is Hittite only; ḱóm 'with, beside' stands for katti=šši 'with him' (not cognate).

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: The serpent had three heads and six eyes.

notes: Watkins ch. 48: THREE-HEADED and SIX-EYED (Av. Aži Dahāka, Ved. Viśvarūpa). The Greek is the three-headed serpent on Agamemnon's shield-strap, with the dative-of-possession construction κεφαλαὶ δέ οἱ ἦσαν τρεῖς that the PIE line uses. Only 'three' is secure (Ved. tri-, Av. θri-, Gk. τρεῖς); 'head' differs (Ved. śīrṣán- < *ḱr̥h₂s-, Gk. κεφαλή), 'six' and 'eye' are Indo-Iranian only, the copula is Greek only, and *h₁ógʷʰis is Indo-Iranian only (Gk. δράκων).

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: The serpent devoured horses and men.

notes: Kərəsāspa's serpent Aži Sruuara, 'horse-devouring, man-devouring' (Y. 9.11 = Yt. 19.40; Watkins ch. 56 on the man-slaying beast); the Homeric snake 'that has devoured' poisonous herbs (Il. 22.93-94). Shared is the root *gʷerh₃- 'devour' (Av. -gar-, Gk. βι-βρώ-σκω). The Avestan compounds become a finite clause with plural objects; horses and men are Avestan only (Ved. gohā́ nṛhā́ in RV 7.56.17 has 'cow' and *gʷʰen-), and *h₁ógʷʰis is Avestan only.
